title: DDL and DML
overview: A DBMS never changes a database by magic: every table it builds is described in its Data Definition Language (DDL), and every look-up, insertion, correction or removal of data is written in its Data Manipulation Language (DML). SQL is the standard language for both. At AS level you must read a given SQL statement and say exactly what it does, write DDL that creates a database and its tables with suitable data types and keys, and write DML scripts over at most two tables using SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT and AVG, plus INSERT INTO, UPDATE and DELETE FROM. This note uses one small sports-centre database (a Member table and a Booking table, continuing the example from 8.1 and 8.2) so that every query can be checked row by row against the data shown.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding that the DBMS carries out all creation/modification of the database structure using its Data Definition Language (DDL).
Show understanding that the DBMS carries out all queries and maintenance of data using its DML.
Show understanding that the industry standard for both DDL and DML is Structured Query Language (SQL), and understand a given SQL statement.

Understand given SQL (DDL) statements and be able to write simple SQL (DDL) statements using a sub-set of statements: CREATE DATABASE; CREATE TABLE with attributes of appropriate data types (CHARACTER, VARCHAR(n), BOOLEAN, INTEGER, REAL, DATE, TIME); ALTER TABLE; PRIMARY KEY (field); FOREIGN KEY (field) REFERENCES Table (Field).

Write an SQL script to query or modify data (DML) which are stored in (at most two) database tables: queries including SELECT ... FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT, AVG; data maintenance including INSERT INTO, DELETE FROM, UPDATE.

definitions.definition: The industry-standard language that relational DBMSs accept for both defining a database's structure (DDL) and querying or maintaining the data in it (DML). Keywords are not case sensitive and each statement ends with a semicolon.

The part of SQL the DBMS uses to create or change the structure of a database: the database itself, its tables, attributes, data types and keys (CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE). DDL puts no data into the tables.
The part of SQL the DBMS uses to work with the data held inside existing tables: reading it with SELECT queries and maintaining it with INSERT INTO, UPDATE and DELETE FROM.
Two text data types. VARCHAR(n) holds a string of any length up to n characters; CHARACTER holds a single character, or with a size such as CHARACTER(4), a string of exactly that fixed length.
The DDL clause, written inside CREATE TABLE or added with ALTER TABLE, that names the attribute whose value must be unique for every record of the table.
The DDL clause that makes an attribute a foreign key, linking it to the primary key of another table, so the DBMS rejects any value that does not already exist in that table.
Part of a SELECT, UPDATE or DELETE FROM statement that gives a condition; only records for which the condition is true are returned, changed or removed.

A function such as SUM, COUNT or AVG that takes the values of one attribute from many records and returns a single value, either for the whole set of selected records or for each group formed by GROUP BY.

A clause that collects together records having the same value in the named attribute(s) so that one output row is produced per group; used with aggregate functions, or on its own to list each value once.

A way of combining two tables in one query: each record in one table is paired with every record in the other whose linking attributes match the ON condition (normally foreign key = primary key); records with no match are left out.

sections.title: SQL: the DBMS's language for structure (DDL) and data (DML)
content: Whatever tools a DBMS shows the user, the work underneath is done through two sets of commands. Anything that creates or alters the structure of the database (the database itself, the tables, the attributes and their data types, and the primary and foreign keys) is carried out by the DBMS using its Data Definition Language. Anything that looks up data, or keeps the stored data up to date by adding, amending or removing records, is carried out using its Data Manipulation Language.

Structured Query Language (SQL) is the industry standard for both. Even when a developer builds a table by clicking in a graphical developer interface, or a user builds a query with a form, the DBMS turns this into SQL. Knowing SQL therefore lets you work with almost any relational DBMS. A few general rules apply to every statement: a script is a sequence of statements; each statement ends with a semicolon and may be spread over several lines; keywords are not case sensitive, though writing them in capitals makes them easy to spot; items in a list are separated by commas.
bullets: DDL = structure: CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES.
DML = data: SELECT queries, and maintenance with INSERT INTO, UPDATE and DELETE FROM.
Quick test: does the statement change which attributes/keys exist (DDL) or which records exist or are returned (DML)?
SQL is the standard for both, so the same statements work, with small dialect differences, across relational DBMSs.

sections.title: CREATE DATABASE and the SQL data types
content: The first DDL statement in a script creates the empty database that the tables will belong to, for example CREATE DATABASE SportsCentre; Nothing else about the structure exists yet.

Each attribute defined later must be given a data type, which tells the DBMS how to store it and which values are allowed. The syllabus uses seven types. Choose the type by what the data really is: a membership code such as M104 is text even though it contains digits, and a telephone number is text because it can start with 0 and is never used in arithmetic.
bullets: Text types: VARCHAR(n) for names and descriptions that vary in length; CHARACTER for one character, or CHARACTER(n) for codes of a fixed length.
Number types: INTEGER for whole numbers (counts, quantities); REAL for numbers with a fractional part (prices, measurements).
BOOLEAN for yes/no facts such as Junior or Paid.
DATE for a calendar date and TIME for a time of day; keep them separate from text so they sort and compare correctly.

examples.label: Choosing a data type for each attribute
examples.content:
Data type  | Holds                                   | Sports-centre example
CHARACTER  | one character, or a fixed-length string | MemberID CHARACTER(4)  e.g. M104
VARCHAR(n) | text of up to n characters              | MemberName VARCHAR(30)
BOOLEAN    | TRUE or FALSE                           | Junior BOOLEAN
INTEGER    | whole number                            | BookingNo INTEGER
REAL       | number with a fractional part           | Fee REAL  e.g. 6.00
DATE       | calendar date                           | DateJoined DATE
TIME       | time of day                             | StartTime TIME

sections.title: CREATE TABLE: attributes, data types and keys
content: CREATE TABLE is followed by the table name and then, inside one pair of brackets, a comma-separated list of attribute definitions, each an attribute name followed by its data type. The keys can be declared inside the same brackets: PRIMARY KEY (field) names the identifying attribute, and FOREIGN KEY (field) REFERENCES Table (Field) links an attribute to the primary key of another table.

In the sports centre, one member can make many bookings, but each booking is for one member. The foreign key MemberID therefore goes in Booking (the 'many' side) and refers to Member's primary key. Member must be created first, because a foreign key can only refer to a table that already exists. Once the tables exist, the DBMS enforces the link: a booking cannot be added for a MemberID that is not in Member.
bullets: Syntax: CREATE TABLE Name ( attribute TYPE, attribute TYPE, ... , PRIMARY KEY (attribute) );
The foreign key goes in the table on the 'many' side and names the table and attribute it refers to.
Create the referenced ('one' side) table before the table holding the foreign key.
DDL only defines the structure: after CREATE TABLE the tables are empty.

examples.label: DDL script for the sports-centre database
examples.content:
CREATE DATABASE SportsCentre;

CREATE TABLE Member (
  MemberID   CHARACTER(4),
  MemberName VARCHAR(30),
  Junior     BOOLEAN,
  DateJoined DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY (MemberID)
);

CREATE TABLE Booking (
  BookingNo  INTEGER,
  MemberID   CHARACTER(4),
  ClassName  VARCHAR(20),
  ClassDate  DATE,
  StartTime  TIME,
  Fee        REAL,
  PRIMARY KEY (BookingNo),
  FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID)
);

sections.title: ALTER TABLE: changing a table definition and adding keys
content: ALTER TABLE changes the definition of a table that already exists, so the table does not have to be deleted and rebuilt. It is used to add a new attribute, and it is also a second way of declaring keys: a table can be created with its attributes only, and the primary and foreign keys added afterwards. Exam questions use both styles, so be ready to write either.
A new attribute added with ALTER TABLE exists for every existing record but holds no value until one is supplied, for example by an UPDATE statement.
bullets: Add an attribute: ALTER TABLE Member ADD Phone VARCHAR(15);
Add a primary key: ALTER TABLE Member ADD PRIMARY KEY (MemberID);
Add a foreign key: ALTER TABLE Booking ADD FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID);
ALTER TABLE is DDL: it changes the table's structure, not the data values stored in it.

examples.label: Defining the same keys with ALTER TABLE instead

sections.title: INSERT INTO: putting data into the tables
content: DML covers three jobs: loading data into the new tables, maintaining it (changing or removing records) and reading it with queries. Loading is done with INSERT INTO, one statement per record. The safer form lists the attribute names and then the matching values, so the statement still works if the column order is not what you expected; the short form gives only the values and relies on them being in the same order as the attributes in the table definition.

Text, date and time values are written inside single quotes; numbers and TRUE/FALSE are not. The syllabus does not fix a date format; this note writes dates as 'YYYY-MM-DD', which cannot be misread and sorts correctly. The eight INSERT INTO statements for Booking, plus four for Member, give the sample data below, which every query in the rest of this note uses. Notice that S. Mensah (M123) has made no bookings.
bullets: Full form: INSERT INTO Table (attr1, attr2, ...) VALUES (value1, value2, ...);
Short form: INSERT INTO Table VALUES (value1, value2, ...); with a value for every attribute in table order.
One INSERT INTO adds one record; the order records were inserted in has no meaning later, so use ORDER BY when order matters.
Insert into the 'one' table (Member) before the 'many' table (Booking), or the foreign key check fails.

examples.label: Two ways to insert a record
Sample data used for every query in this note

sections.title: SELECT ... FROM with WHERE and ORDER BY
content: A query always begins with SELECT, followed by the attributes to output, then FROM and the table to read. SELECT * outputs every attribute. A WHERE clause adds a condition, so only records for which it is true are output; conditions can use =, <>, <, >, <=, >= and be combined with AND and OR. ORDER BY sorts the output by the named attribute, ascending (ASC) unless DESC is written.

WHERE decides which records appear; ORDER BY only decides the order they appear in. Comparisons on DATE and TIME values work in time order, so WHERE DateJoined < '2025-01-01' means 'joined before 2025'.
bullets: Attributes in the SELECT list are separated by commas, with no brackets.
Text literals in quotes ('Yoga'); numbers without (7.00); BOOLEAN values as TRUE or FALSE.
ORDER BY attribute DESC gives largest/latest first; ASC (the default) gives smallest/earliest or A to Z first.
Only the attributes listed after SELECT are output, even if WHERE tests a different attribute.

examples.label: Three queries and their exact results
examples.content:
Query A
SELECT MemberID, MemberName
FROM Member
WHERE Junior = TRUE
ORDER BY MemberName;

Junior is TRUE for M117 and M123. Sorted A to Z by name:
MemberID | MemberName
M117     | L. Ortiz
M123     | S. Mensah

Query B
SELECT MemberName, DateJoined
FROM Member
WHERE DateJoined < '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY DateJoined;

Joined before 2025: M104 (2024-03-15) and M120 (2023-11-20). Earliest first:
MemberName | DateJoined
T. Reyes   | 2023-11-20
O. Haddad  | 2024-03-15

Query C
SELECT BookingNo, ClassName, Fee
FROM Booking
WHERE MemberID = 'M104' AND Fee >= 7.00
ORDER BY Fee DESC;

M104's bookings are 1 (6.00), 2 (8.00), 5 (7.00), 8 (6.00); only 2 and 5 have Fee >= 7.00:
BookingNo | ClassName | Fee
2         | Spin      | 8.00
5         | Pilates   | 7.00

sections.title: GROUP BY and the aggregate functions SUM, COUNT and AVG
content: SUM, COUNT and AVG each take many records and return one value. COUNT(*) counts records; SUM(attribute) adds up a numeric attribute; AVG(attribute) gives its mean. Without GROUP BY, the function works over every record that passes the WHERE clause and the query outputs a single row.

GROUP BY puts records with the same value of the named attribute into one group and outputs one row per group, so an aggregate function is worked out separately for each group. Any attribute in the SELECT list that is not inside an aggregate function must also appear in GROUP BY, because it has to have one value per group. GROUP BY can also be used with no aggregate at all to list each value once, for example the members who have made at least one booking. The WHERE clause is applied first, to individual records, before the groups are formed.
bullets: COUNT(*) counts records; SUM(Fee) totals; AVG(Fee) = SUM(Fee) / COUNT of the records used.
Order of work: FROM, then WHERE removes records, then GROUP BY forms groups, then each aggregate is calculated per group, then ORDER BY sorts the output rows.
Every non-aggregated attribute in SELECT must be listed in GROUP BY.
SELECT MemberID FROM Booking GROUP BY MemberID; lists each member with a booking once, instead of once per booking.

examples.label: Aggregates over the Booking table, calculated by hand
examples.content:
Query D (whole table, no GROUP BY)
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(Fee), AVG(Fee)
FROM Booking;

COUNT = 8 records
SUM   = 6.00 + 8.00 + 6.00 + 7.00 + 7.00 + 8.00 + 6.00 + 6.00 = 54.00
AVG   = 54.00 / 8 = 6.75
COUNT(*) | SUM(Fee) | AVG(Fee)
8        | 54.00    | 6.75

Query E (one row per class)
SELECT ClassName, COUNT(*), SUM(Fee)
FROM Booking
GROUP BY ClassName
ORDER BY ClassName;

Pilates: bookings 4, 5        -> 2 records, 7.00 + 7.00 = 14.00
Spin:    bookings 2, 6        -> 2 records, 8.00 + 8.00 = 16.00
Yoga:    bookings 1, 3, 7, 8  -> 4 records, 4 x 6.00   = 24.00
ClassName | COUNT(*) | SUM(Fee)
Pilates   | 2        | 14.00
Spin      | 2        | 16.00
Yoga      | 4        | 24.00

Query F (WHERE before GROUP BY)
SELECT MemberID, AVG(Fee)
FROM Booking
WHERE ClassName <> 'Yoga'
GROUP BY MemberID
ORDER BY MemberID;

WHERE keeps bookings 2, 4, 5, 6 only.
M104: bookings 2, 5 -> (8.00 + 7.00) / 2 = 7.50
M117: booking 6     -> 8.00 / 1 = 8.00
M120: booking 4     -> 7.00 / 1 = 7.00
MemberID | AVG(Fee)
M104     | 7.50
M117     | 8.00
M120     | 7.00

Query G (GROUP BY to list each value once)
SELECT MemberID FROM Booking GROUP BY MemberID ORDER BY MemberID;
MemberID
M104
M117
M120
(M123 has no bookings, so it cannot appear.)

sections.title: INNER JOIN: a query over two tables
content: When the output needs attributes from both tables, such as a member's name (in Member) next to the class booked (in Booking), the tables are combined with INNER JOIN. The ON condition says which records belong together: the foreign key in one table must equal the primary key it refers to in the other, here Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID. Each Booking record is paired with the one Member record that has the same MemberID.

Because both tables contain an attribute called MemberID, attributes are written in full as Table.Attribute to make clear which table each comes from. An inner join only outputs pairs that match, so a member with no bookings (S. Mensah) never appears in a joined result. WHERE, GROUP BY, the aggregate functions and ORDER BY can all be used on the joined records exactly as on a single table. Some texts write the join condition in the WHERE clause instead of using INNER JOIN ... ON; the result is the same, but the INNER JOIN form is the one the syllabus names.
bullets: Syntax: SELECT T1.a, T2.b FROM T1 INNER JOIN T2 ON T1.key = T2.key;
The ON condition matches the foreign key to the primary key it references, not any two attributes that happen to look alike.
Unmatched records (a member with no bookings) are left out of an inner join.
The syllabus limits queries to at most two tables, so one INNER JOIN is the most you will need.

examples.label: Joined queries with their exact results
examples.content:
Query H
SELECT Member.MemberName, Booking.ClassName, Booking.ClassDate
FROM Member
INNER JOIN Booking ON Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID
WHERE Member.Junior = TRUE
ORDER BY Booking.ClassDate;

Junior members: M117 and M123. M117 matches bookings 3 and 6; M123 matches none.
MemberName | ClassName | ClassDate
L. Ortiz   | Yoga      | 2026-10-05
L. Ortiz   | Spin      | 2026-10-06

Query I (join + GROUP BY + COUNT)
SELECT Member.MemberName, COUNT(*)
FROM Member
INNER JOIN Booking ON Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID
GROUP BY Member.MemberName
ORDER BY Member.MemberName;

O. Haddad (M104): bookings 1, 2, 5, 8 -> 4
L. Ortiz  (M117): bookings 3, 6       -> 2
T. Reyes  (M120): bookings 4, 7       -> 2
S. Mensah (M123): no matching booking -> no row
MemberName | COUNT(*)
L. Ortiz   | 2
O. Haddad  | 4
T. Reyes   | 2

sections.title: UPDATE and DELETE FROM: maintaining the data
content: UPDATE changes values in records that already exist: the table name, then SET with the new value(s), then a WHERE clause picking out the records to change. DELETE FROM removes whole records that match a WHERE clause; the table and its structure remain. In both, the WHERE clause is what limits the change. Leave it out and every record in the table is updated or deleted.

Referential integrity affects the order of deletions. A member cannot be removed while Booking still holds records whose foreign key refers to that member, so the DBMS rejects the delete. Remove the member's bookings first, then the member.
bullets: UPDATE Table SET attribute = value WHERE condition;  (several changes: SET a = 1, b = 2)
DELETE FROM Table WHERE condition;  removes whole records, never single attribute values.
No WHERE clause means every record is affected.
Delete from the 'many' table before the 'one' table when removing linked data.

examples.label: Maintaining the sample data, with the effect of each statement

sections.title: Understanding a given SQL statement
content: Many questions give you a statement and ask what it does or what it outputs. First decide whether it is DDL (it creates or changes structure: say which table, attributes, types or keys) or DML. For a query, work through the clauses in the order the DBMS applies them rather than the order they are written: FROM and any INNER JOIN say which records are available; WHERE removes records; GROUP BY forms groups; SUM, COUNT or AVG are worked out per group; SELECT picks the attributes to output; ORDER BY sorts.

When sample data is given, list the records that survive each step, write the output as a table with the column headings, and check the number of rows. Describing the output in words, when the question asks for the result, will not earn the marks.
bullets: DDL question: name the table, each attribute with its type, and each key and what it references.
Query question: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, aggregates, SELECT, ORDER BY.
Write the result as rows with headings, in the order ORDER BY gives.
Check for traps: an inner join drops unmatched records; WHERE on text is an exact match; a missing WHERE affects every record.

examples.label: Tracing a given two-table query step by step
examples.content:
SELECT Member.MemberName, SUM(Booking.Fee)
FROM Member
INNER JOIN Booking ON Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID
WHERE Member.Junior = FALSE
GROUP BY Member.MemberName
ORDER BY SUM(Booking.Fee) DESC;

1. FROM/JOIN: each of the 8 bookings is paired with its member (M123 has none).
2. WHERE: keep non-junior members only: M104 (bookings 1, 2, 5, 8) and M120 (bookings 4, 7).
3. GROUP BY: two groups, O. Haddad and T. Reyes.
4. SUM: O. Haddad 6.00 + 8.00 + 7.00 + 6.00 = 27.00; T. Reyes 7.00 + 6.00 = 13.00.
5. ORDER BY ... DESC: largest total first.

MemberName | SUM(Booking.Fee)
O. Haddad  | 27.00
T. Reyes   | 13.00

In words: the total spent on bookings by each adult (non-junior) member, highest spender first.

comparisonTable.title: SQL statements in the syllabus: DDL and DML
rows: Defines a table's attributes, data types and keys
CREATE TABLE Member (MemberID CHARACTER(4), ..., PRIMARY KEY (MemberID));
Changes an existing table definition: adds an attribute or a key
ALTER TABLE Member ADD Phone VARCHAR(15);
Queries data, optionally with WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, INNER JOIN, SUM/COUNT/AVG
SELECT MemberName FROM Member WHERE Junior = TRUE;
Changes values in existing records that match WHERE
UPDATE Booking SET Fee = 7.50 WHERE ClassName = 'Pilates';
Removes existing records that match WHERE

diagram.title: From DDL script to DML queries
nodes: CREATE TABLE Member (PK MemberID) - the 'one' side first
CREATE TABLE Booking (PK BookingNo, FK MemberID REFERENCES Member)
ALTER TABLE if the design changes (new attribute or key)
INSERT INTO: load Member records, then Booking records
SELECT ... FROM ... INNER JOIN ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... ORDER BY to query
UPDATE / DELETE FROM with WHERE to maintain the data

analysisChains.title: Why a delete is rejected
steps: The DBA runs DELETE FROM Member WHERE MemberID = 'M120';
Booking was created with FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID)
Bookings 4 and 7 still hold MemberID M120, so removing M120 would leave them referring to a member who does not exist
The DBMS enforces referential integrity and rejects the statement; Member is unchanged
analysisChains.evaluation: The DDL written when the table was created controls what the DML may later do. The fix is to delete (or reassign) the member's bookings first, then delete the member.

analysisChains.title: Where the WHERE clause goes in an aggregate query
steps: Task: the average fee per member, ignoring Yoga bookings
WHERE ClassName <> 'Yoga' removes bookings 1, 3, 7 and 8 before any grouping happens
GROUP BY MemberID then forms groups from bookings 2, 4, 5, 6 only
analysisChains.evaluation: Because WHERE acts on single records before groups are formed, leaving out the condition would change M104's average to 27.00 / 4 = 6.75. Always apply the WHERE step first when working out an aggregate by hand.

analysisChains.title: Why a member disappears from a joined result
steps: Query I counts bookings per member using Member INNER JOIN Booking ON Member.MemberID = Booking.MemberID
M123 (S. Mensah) is in Member but no Booking record has MemberID M123
An inner join only outputs pairs where the ON condition is true, so M123 produces no joined record at all
The result has three rows, not four, and there is no row showing S. Mensah with a count of 0
analysisChains.evaluation: When predicting the output of a joined query, check every record for a match; records without one are silently left out. A question asking for 'all members' cannot be answered completely by an inner join on Booking.

examTips: Write SQL keywords in capitals, lay each clause on its own line, and end every statement with a semicolon; the marks are for exact syntax.
In CREATE TABLE, give every attribute a data type from the syllabus list and put the key clauses in the form PRIMARY KEY (field) and FOREIGN KEY (field) REFERENCES Table(Field).
Use the attribute names exactly as the question spells them, and use Table.Attribute in any query with INNER JOIN.
When asked for the output of a query, write the actual rows with column headings, in ORDER BY order, checked against the given data.
Put text, date and time values in single quotes; leave numbers and TRUE/FALSE unquoted.
commonMistakes: Calling SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE a DDL statement; they act on data, so they are DML.
Storing codes or phone numbers as INTEGER; values such as M104, or a phone number starting with 0, are text (CHARACTER or VARCHAR).
Leaving out WHERE in UPDATE or DELETE FROM, which changes or removes every record in the table.
Selecting a non-aggregated attribute that is not listed in GROUP BY, e.g. SELECT ClassName, MemberID, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY ClassName.
Writing the INNER JOIN ON condition with the wrong attributes, such as Member.MemberID = Booking.BookingNo, instead of foreign key = primary key.
Forgetting that WHERE is applied before GROUP BY, so aggregates are calculated only from the records that passed the condition.

quickRecall.question: Which part of the DBMS's language creates or changes the database structure, and which queries and maintains the data?
quickRecall.answer: DDL creates/modifies the structure (CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, keys); DML queries and maintains data (SELECT, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE FROM).

quickRecall.question: What is the industry standard language for both DDL and DML?
Name the seven data types listed in the syllabus.
quickRecall.answer: CHARACTER, VARCHAR(n), BOOLEAN, INTEGER, REAL, DATE, TIME.

quickRecall.question: Write the DDL to make MemberID in Booking a foreign key to Member.
quickRecall.answer: ALTER TABLE Booking ADD FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID); (or the FOREIGN KEY clause inside CREATE TABLE Booking).

quickRecall.question: Using the sample Booking data, what does SELECT ClassName, COUNT(*) FROM Booking GROUP BY ClassName ORDER BY ClassName; output?
What is output by SELECT AVG(Fee) FROM Booking; on the sample data?
Why does S. Mensah never appear in a query that uses Member INNER JOIN Booking?
quickRecall.answer: She has no Booking records, and an inner join only outputs records whose ON condition finds a match.

quickRecall.question: What happens if UPDATE Booking SET Fee = 7.50; is run without a WHERE clause?
quickRecall.answer: Every booking's Fee becomes 7.50, not just the intended records.
